articles.title: The Remote Support Appliance Was Open for Seven Weeks - CVE-2026-102764 and What ARMORY CASTLE Left Behind
articles.nav_title: The Remote Support Appliance Was Open for Seven Weeks
articles.home_blurb: A remote support appliance reaches every machine you support, with the credentials to do it. CVE-2026-102764, a critical BeyondTrust auth bypass, let the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE onto it as a zero-day from late August 2026. The vulnerability is one sentence; what they built on the box - a 404-answering web shell, a tunnel hidden behind the appliance's own proxy, root persistence that survives a config reset - is the part to read.
articles.card_blurb: CVE-2026-102764 is a CVSS 9.3 authentication bypass in BeyondTrust Remote Support, exploited as a zero-day since late August 2026 by ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221). The timeline, the SAWFLY web shell that returns 404 to scanners, the BARECLAW SOCKS5-over-WebSocket tunnel hidden via HAProxy, SUID and sudoers persistence, anti-forensic log deletion, the hashes and YARA Mandiant published, and why patching does not remove persistence.
articles.feed_desc: CVE-2026-102764 is an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290) in BeyondTrust Remote Support, CVSS v4.0 9.3, letting an unauthenticated remote attacker perform file operations on the appliance. It was exploited as a zero-day from late August 2026 by ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221; CrowdStrike Warp Panda), a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor; affects all supported versions up to 26.2.3, patch BT26-05-RS, SaaS patched 9 October, Privileged Remote Access shares the code, CISA KEV 16 October. The dated timeline, the SAWFLY web shell (mangoapi.php, 404 scanner evasion), the BARECLAW tunneler hidden behind the appliance HAProxy config, root persistence via a SUID shell and a sudoers template, log-deletion anti-forensics and the tell it leaves, the published SHA-256 hashes and YARA rules, a full hunt table, the ATT&CK mapping, and why patching does not remove persistence.

articles.title: When the Allowlist Isn't a Boundary - Auto-Approve Bypasses in an Abandoned AI Coding Agent
articles.nav_title: When the Allowlist Isn't a Boundary
articles.home_blurb: An AI coding agent that can run shell commands keeps an allowlist of commands it runs without asking. Five disclosed Roo Code flaws (CVE-2026-110202 to 110206) show the list was never a wall: the code that checks the command and the shell that runs it read it differently. The instruction can arrive by indirect prompt injection, and there is no patch - the project was archived in May.
articles.card_blurb: Five command auto-approve bypasses in Roo Code (CVE-2026-110202 through 110206), all through version 3.54.0, let a command pass the allowlist check and then run something else in the shell. The delivery is indirect prompt injection, no local access needed; every bypass needs auto-approval on. There is no fix - the repository was archived on 15 May 2026. Why a command allowlist is not a security boundary, how it maps to excessive agency and the confused deputy, and what a defender does about an unmaintained AI agent.
articles.feed_desc: On 13 October 2026 VulnCheck disclosed five command auto-approve bypasses in Roo Code, an open-source AI coding agent for VS Code: CVE-2026-110202 through CVE-2026-110206, all affecting versions through 3.54.0. Each is a parser-differential: the checker that judges a command against the auto-approve allowlist and the shell that executes it disagree, so a command passes the check and runs something the allowlist would deny. The trigger is indirect prompt injection - text planted in content the agent reads - and all five require auto-approval enabled. There is no fixed release: the repository was archived on 15 May 2026 and is read-only. The five bypasses at a defender's depth, how this is excessive agency plus indirect injection plus the confused deputy with the one containing control removed, why it is hard to detect and the endpoint behaviour to watch instead, the ATT&CK and ATLAS mapping, and the response to an unmaintained AI agent.

articles.title: php2shell and the Hallucinated Exploit - What Defenders Should Actually Do About CVE-2026-109618/109619
articles.home_blurb: There is a real unauthenticated RCE in PHP, patched on 21 October 2026. There is also a flood of "php2shell" PoCs on GitHub and in honeypot traffic, and most are not that bug at all - they are a 2018 session-poisoning trick an LLM mistook for the CVE because both touch PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. Telling the two apart is this week's job.
articles.card_blurb: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are two critical memory-safety bugs allowing unauthenticated RCE in PHP itself, patched 21 October 2026 in 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35. But most public PoCs are a 2018 session-poisoning plus LFI technique a language model confused for the real flaw. The real bug, why exploitation is hard, what the telemetry actually says, how to detect attempts without letting an LLM triage them, and why accurate threat intel is not downplaying.
articles.feed_desc: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 ("php2shell") are two critical memory-safety bugs in PHP's request handling that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution before application code runs, highest risk on Apache mod_php, CVSS v4.0 9.2, fixed on 21 October 2026 in 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35. Yet most PoCs on GitHub and in honeypot traffic are the unrelated 2018 PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS session-poisoning technique, generated by people feeding loose CVE details into an LLM that keyed on the shared feature name. The real bugs at a defender's depth, why RCE is genuinely hard, what Amazon MadPot and other telemetry actually show (attempts, not confirmed success, not yet in CISA KEV), a low-confidence request tripwire and the worker-crash hunt that is harder to fake, mitigations including CVE-2026-115560, and why reporting what you see is not downplaying.

articles.title: Sixteen Days From KEV to Exfiltration - What the Mathspace Breach Says About Internal Tooling
articles.nav_title: Sixteen Days From KEV to Exfiltration
articles.home_blurb: Metabase patched an unauthenticated SQL injection on 6 August 2026 and said the flaw was already being exploited. CISA listed it on 11 August. On 27 August, 1,079,819 records left an Australian platform's self-hosted instance. Every date was public before the data moved - the failure was that nothing connected the advisory to the asset.
articles.card_blurb: CVE-2026-72898 turns Metabase's password reset endpoint into unauthenticated administrator access, and a BI tool is pre-joined access to everything it is credentialed to reach. Patch available 6 August, intrusion 10 August, CISA KEV 11 August, data gone 27 August. The timeline, what the CVSS vectors predicted, a Sigma rule and a hunt, and why this was an inventory failure rather than a patching one.
articles.feed_desc: CVE-2026-72898 is an unauthenticated SQL injection in Metabase's /api/session/reset_password endpoint, CVSS 10.0 under both v3.1 and v4.0, yielding administrator access to the instance and through it every database it holds. Metabase confirmed active exploitation when it published the fix on 6 August 2026; CISA added the CVE to KEV on 11 August; an Australian edtech platform's self-hosted instance was accessed on 10 August and 1,079,819 records were downloaded on 27 August. The verified timeline, what S:C in the CVSS vector told you in advance, one Sigma rule plus a volume and egress hunt, the ATT&CK mapping, and why asset discovery rather than patch speed is the control that failed.

articles.feed_desc: CVE-2026-18556 and CVE-2026-18577 are authentication bypasses in N-able N-central, an RMM platform used by MSPs to manage client fleets. Both were added to CISA KEV in early August 2026 after in-the-wild exploitation, and the second exists because the fix for the first was incomplete. For an organisation with outsourced IT the vulnerable server is not theirs to patch - but the Take Control sessions, the svchost.exe dropped into a user's Documents folder, and the Cloudflared persistence service all executed on their endpoints. The timeline, what the published CVSS vectors tell a defender, two Sigma rules, a hunt procedure, and the supplier questions that follow.
